questions.q: Which sentence describes a library?
questions.explain: Your loop called formatPrice; formatPrice did not know the loop existed. With a library, the control flow is yours. With a framework, it is the other way round.
options: Code that you call, when you decide; your code stays in charge of the flow
Code that calls your functions when it decides the time is right
Code that must be installed globally with npm install -g
Code that only runs inside a web browser, never on a server

questions.q: What is inversion of control?
questions.explain: With a framework, you write pieces and the framework calls them at the right time. It is often summed up as "don't call us, we'll call you".
options: Your code calls the framework's functions in reverse order
You hand pieces to the framework, and the framework decides when to call them
The framework reverses the order of the modules on every start
The client controls the server instead of the server controlling the client

questions.q: Which part of the BookStore already used inversion of control?
questions.explain: You gave handlers to the router and never called them yourself. The router decided when, based on the incoming request. That is exactly how a framework treats your code.
options: The formatPrice helper that the handlers called
The SQL query that loaded a book by its id
The router, which called your handlers when a request arrived
The Number() calls that parsed each setting

questions.q: Why does the lesson say inversion of control is "not a loss"?
questions.explain: Giving up the control flow means giving up a lot of tedious, risky work: ordering, error handling, shutdown. The framework has done that work a thousand times before.
options: Because you can always turn it off again with a setting
Because a framework runs your code faster than you could
Because you still decide when every one of your functions runs
Code called at the right time and order by tested code is code you no longer write

questions.q: startOrder puts every module after the modules it depends on. What is this kind of ordering called?
questions.explain: Visiting each module's dependencies before the module itself gives a topological sort: an order where every item comes after the things it needs.
options: A binary search
A topological sort
A reverse sort
An alphabetical sort

questions.q: What is the visiting set in startOrder for?
questions.explain: visiting holds the modules whose dependencies are being visited right now. Meeting one of them again means a loop that can never start, so the framework throws a clear error.
options: It remembers which modules have already been started
It stores the modules in the order they must be stopped
It notices a cycle: meeting a module still being visited means A needs B needs A
It counts how many times each module is listed as a dependency

questions.q: Why does stop walk the started modules in reverse?
questions.explain: The server must stop taking requests before the database it uses is closed. Reverse start order guarantees that every module stops while the things it needs are still running.
options: So a module stops before what it depends on, like the server before its database
Because the last module started is always the slowest one to stop
Because JavaScript arrays are faster to read from the end
So that the modules stop in alphabetical order of their names

questions.q: What does await module.start?.(); do when a module has no start function?
questions.explain: Optional chaining calls the function only if it exists. A module without start is simply skipped, and await undefined continues at once.
options: It throws TypeError: module.start is not a function
Nothing: ?. skips the call and gives undefined
It calls a default start that the framework provides
It waits forever, because there is nothing to await

questions.q: In the mini framework, http needs database, and database needs cache, which is not registered. When is the mistake found?
questions.explain: start first computes the whole order with startOrder, which throws on a missing dependency. A broken setup is refused before anything runs.
options: Only when the first request reaches the http module
After http and database have started
Before any module starts, while the start order is worked out
Never; the missing module is silently skipped

questions.q: orders needs payments, payments needs mailer, and mailer needs orders. How do you fix it?
questions.explain: In a cycle none of the modules can go first, and the listing order does not change the dependencies. Break the loop by moving what they share into a module with no dependency back on them.
options: List the three modules in a different order in createApp
Remove the stop functions from all three modules
Start all three modules at the same time instead
Move the shared part into a new module that the others depend on

questions.q: What is a rollback when an app starts?
questions.explain: Without rollback, a failed database start leaves the config module (and others) running and never stopped. @zudojs/runtime does this for you.
options: Starting the modules again from the first one after a failure
When one module fails to start, stopping the ones already started, in reverse
Going back to the previous version of the app's code
Ignoring the failed module and starting all the others

questions.q: Which ZudoJS packages take over the lifecycle job: start in order, stop in reverse, react to SIGTERM, report readiness?
questions.explain: Runtime and lifecycle start and stop your parts in the right order and undo a half-finished start. The container handles dependency injection, not start order.
options: @zudojs/container
@zudojs/runtime and @zudojs/lifecycle
@zudojs/http and @zudojs/middleware
@zudojs/config

questions.q: In the BookStore, createRouter built every repository and passed the secret through by hand. What does a container give you instead?
questions.explain: A dependency-injection container knows how to build each service and hands it out where needed. In ZudoJS it is @zudojs/container.
options: A Docker image that runs the whole app
A folder where every class file must live
Register each service once, and ask for it by name wherever it is needed
A single global object that every file may change

questions.q: What does a framework's validation give you, compared with the BookStore's hand-written parsers?
questions.explain: In the BookStore, the parser and the interface were written separately and could drift apart. A schema (@zudojs/schema) is one description that gives both. TypeScript types alone never check data at runtime.
options: It removes the need to check any input
Describe the data once, and get both the runtime check and the TypeScript type
It checks the types at compile time, so no runtime check is needed
It turns every string in the body into a number automatically

questions.q: What does a framework's configuration job include?
questions.explain: @zudojs/config merges several sources, checks them, and keeps secrets out of logs. Secrets never belong in source code or log lines.
options: Writing every secret directly into the source code
Reading one environment variable at a time, with no types
Layered sources (defaults, files, environment), types, validation, and secrets hidden from logs
Printing all settings, including passwords, at startup

questions.q: The BookStore had no rate limit and no security headers. Which ZudoJS package gives you rate limiting, CORS, CSRF and security headers with safe defaults?
questions.explain: @zudojs/security covers these, and @zudojs/auth covers password hashing and JWTs. Using tested, safe defaults is better than writing each one by hand.
options: @zudojs/errors
@zudojs/schema
@zudojs/security
@zudojs/testing

questions.q: What does a framework give you for application architecture?
questions.explain: In the BookStore you chose folders and layers yourself. A standard layout from zudojs-cli means any developer can find their way in any project.
options: Every project gets its own unique folder layout
It removes the need for layers like domain and infrastructure
A standard project layout and modules, created by a CLI, so every project looks alike
A diagram of the app, drawn at every start

questions.q: Which is a real cost of using a framework?
questions.explain: The lesson names three costs: learning time, the framework's opinions about structure, and depending on its future. Pick one that is maintained and whose parts you can replace.
options: You can no longer use TypeScript
Your app can no longer use a database
You must learn its names and rules, and work its way when your problem does not fit
You must write the lifecycle and the routing yourself anyway

questions.q: For which project is a backend framework most likely too much?
questions.explain: For a small script, learning a framework costs more than it saves. For a real backend, the jobs a framework does must be done anyway, by it or by you.
options: A 50-line script that renames some files once
An API with users, a database and several developers
A shop backend that runs on a production server
A service that must shut down cleanly on SIGTERM

questions.q: Finish startOrder so every module comes after the modules it depends on (visit the dependencies first, then push the module, and skip a module that is already in the list). Return the names.
questions.explain: A recursive visit handles the dependencies before the module itself. The includes check stops a module from being added twice when several modules need it.

questions.q: Finish checkDependencies(modules). It returns a list of messages "A needs B", one for every dependency B of a module A that is not registered. Return an empty list when all is fine.
questions.explain: Put the registered names in a Set, then check every dependency of every module. Remember that dependsOn is optional, so use ?? [].

questions.q: Finish startOrder so it throws Error('Circular dependency at "NAME"') when it meets a module that is still being visited. Use the visiting set.
questions.explain: Check visiting before adding the module to it. Without that check, a cycle would make visit call itself forever until the stack overflows.

questions.q: Finish createApp(modules). start() starts the modules in the given order and remembers the started ones. stop() stops the started modules in reverse, then forgets them. Modules without start or stop are allowed.

questions.q: Finish the tiny framework createRouter. on(path, handler) registers a handler. handle(path) calls the matching handler and returns its result, or returns "404 not found" when no handler matches.
questions.explain: Your handlers are only stored by on; the router decides when to call them. That is the "we'll call you" side of inversion of control.
